'''''Alliaria petiolata''''', or  '''garlic mustard''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> is a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the mustard family ([[Brassicaceae]]). It is native to Europe, western and central Asia, north-western Africa, [[Morocco]], [[Iberian Peninsula|Iberia]] and the [[British Isles]], north to northern [[Scandinavia]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Flora Europaea|publisher= Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh|url=http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Alliaria&SPECIES_XREF=&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK=}}</ref> and east to northern [[Pakistan]] and [[Xinjiang]] in western China.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:1176324-2|title=''Alliaria petiolata'' (M.Bieb.) Cavara & Grande | Plants of the World Online | Kew Science|website=powo.science.kew.org|access-date=1 May 2022}}</ref> It has now become a tenacious [[invasive species|invasive plant]] across the northern U.S., in particular because of its earlier springtime emergence than many native species, often in the forest [[understory]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nature.org/en-us/about-us/where-we-work/united-states/indiana/stories-in-indiana/garlic-mustard/ |title=What is Garlic Mustard? |date=25 October 2024 |website=The Nature Conservancy |access-date=6 May 2025}}</ref>

In the first year of growth, plants form clumps of round, slightly wrinkled leaves, that when crushed smell like garlic. The plants flower in spring of the next year, producing cross-shaped white flowers in dense clusters. As the flowering stems bloom they elongate into a spike-like shape. When flowering is complete, plants produce upright fruits that release seeds in mid-summer. Plants are often found growing along the margins of [[hedge]]s, giving rise to the old British folk name of '''jack-by-the-hedge'''. Other common names include '''garlic root''', '''hedge garlic''', '''sauce-alone''', '''jack-in-the-bush''', '''penny hedge''' and '''poor man's mustard'''. The genus name ''Alliaria'', "resembling ''[[Allium]]''", refers to the [[garlic]]-like odour of the crushed foliage. All parts of the plant, including the roots, have this smell.

==Description==
It is an herbaceous [[biennial plant]]<ref name="tfb">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=61}}</ref> growing from a deeply growing, thin, whitish taproot scented like [[horseradish]]. In their first years, plants are [[Rosette_(botany)|rosettes]] of green leaves close to the ground; these rosettes remain green through the winter and develop into mature flowering plants the following spring. Second-year plants often grow from {{convert|30–100|cm|abbr=on}} tall, rarely to {{convert|130|cm|abbr=on}} tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are stalked, triangular through heart-shaped,<ref name="tfb" /> {{convert|10-15|cm|abbr=on}} long (of which about half being the [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]) and {{convert|5-9|cm|abbr=on|1}} broad, with coarsely toothed margins. The [[flower]]s are produced in spring and summer in small clusters. Each small flower has four white petals<ref name="tfb" /> {{convert|4-8|mm|abbr=on|1}} long and {{convert|2-3|mm|abbr=on|2}} broad, arranged in a cross shape. The [[fruit]] is an erect, slender, four-sided capsule {{convert|4-5.5|cm|abbr=on|1}} long,<ref>{{cite web | title=Invader of the Month – Garlic Mustard – ''Alliaria petiolata'' | url=http://www.hort.uconn.edu/cipwg/invader_month/invader_of_the_month_Mar06_alliaria.pdf | access-date=2009-05-21 | archive-date=9 June 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150609061812/http://www.hort.uconn.edu/cipwg/invader_month/invader_of_the_month_Mar06_alliaria.pdf }}</ref> called a [[silique]], green maturing to pale grey brown, containing two rows of small shiny black [[seed]]s which are released when a silique splits open. A single plant can produce hundreds of seeds, which often scatter several meters from the parent plant.

Depending upon conditions, garlic mustard flowers either [[Autogamy|self-fertilize]] or are [[cross-pollinated]] by a variety of insects.
[[File:(MHNT) Alliaria petiolata - flowers.jpg|thumb|Close-up of garlic mustard flowers]]
[[File:Alliaria petiolataseeds.jpg|thumb|right|Garlic mustard seeds]]

Sixty-nine insect herbivores and seven fungi are associated with garlic mustard in Europe. The most important groups of natural enemies associated with garlic mustard were [[weevil]]s (particularly the genus ''[[Ceutorhynchus]]''), [[leaf beetles]], [[butterflies]], and [[moths]], including the [[larva]]e of some moth species such as the [[garden carpet]] moth.<ref name="Garlic Mustard">{{cite book |last1=Blossey |first1=Bernd |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/foresthealth/technology/pdfs/BiocontrolsOfInvasivePlants02_04.pdf |title=Biological Control of Invasive Plants in the Eastern United States |last2=Nuzzo |first2=Victoria A. |last3=Hinz |first3=Hariet L. |last4=Gerber |first4=Esther |date=August 2002 |publisher=USDA Forest Service |editor1-last=Van Driesche |editor1-first=Roy |pages=365–372 |chapter=Garlic Mustard |citeseerx=10.1.1.96.3575 |editor2-last=Blossey |editor2-first=Bernd |editor3-last=Hoddle |editor3-first=Mark |editor4-last=Lyon |editor4-first=Suzanne |editor5-last=Reardon |editor5-first=Richard}}</ref> The small white flowers have a rather unpleasant aroma which attracts [[midge]]s and [[hoverfly|hoverflies]], although the flowers usually pollinate themselves. In June the pale green caterpillar of the [[Anthocharis cardamines|orange tip butterfly]] (''Anthocharis cardamines'') can be found feeding on the long green seed-pods from which it can hardly be distinguished.<ref name="Reader 2001"/>

== Invasiveness in North America ==
{{main|Garlic mustard as an invasive species}}

Garlic mustard was introduced to North America by European settlers in the 1800s for culinary and medicinal purposes.<ref name="nvca">{{cite web |title=Garlic Mustard Monitoring Along the Bruce Trail in the Nottawasaga Valley Watershed |url=https://www.nvca.on.ca/Shared%20Documents/Garlic%20Mustard%20Monitoring%20Along%20the%20Bruce%20Trail%20in%20the%20Nottawasaga%20Valley.pdf |access-date=18 March 2026 |publisher=Nottawasaga Valley Conservation Authority |archive-date=22 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151022171210/https://www.nvca.on.ca/Shared%20Documents/Garlic%20Mustard%20Monitoring%20Along%20the%20Bruce%20Trail%20in%20the%20Nottawasaga%20Valley.pdf |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref> The species was recorded as being in [[Long Island]] in 1868.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lyle |first1=Katie Letcher |title=Complete guide to edible wild plants, mushrooms, fruits, and nuts: how to find, identify, and cook them |date=2010 |publisher=FalconGuides |isbn=978-1-59921-887-8 |page=17 |oclc=560560606}}</ref> It has since spread all over North America, apart from the far south of the US and some prairie states and Canadian provinces.<ref name="ow">{{cite web |title=''Alliaria petiolata'' |url=http://ontariowildflowers.com/main/species.php?id=163 |access-date=3 May 2018 |website=Ontario Wildflowers}}</ref> It is toxic or unpalatable to many native herbivores, as well as to some native [[Lepidoptera]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Haribal |first1=Meena |last2=Renwick |first2=J.Alan A. |date=April 1998 |title=Isovitexin 6"-O-β-d-glucopyranoside: A feeding deterrent to ''Pieris napi oleracea'' from ''Alliaria petiolata'' |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=47 |issue=7 |pages=1237–1240 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(97)00740-1 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Daxenbichler |first1=Melvin E. |last2=Spencer |first2=Gayland F. |last3=Carlson |first3=Diana G. |last4=Rose |first4=Gertrude B. |last5=Brinker |first5=Anita M. |last6=Powell |first6=Richard G. |date=January 1991 |title=Glucosinolate composition of seeds from 297 species of wild plants |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=30 |issue=8 |pages=2623–2638 |bibcode=1991PChem..30.2623D |doi=10.1016/0031-9422(91)85112-d}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cipollini |first1=D. |date=1 September 2002 |title=Variation in the expression of chemical defenses in ''Alliaria petiolata'' (Brassicaceae) in the field and common garden |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=89 |issue=9 |pages=1422–1430 |doi=10.3732/ajb.89.9.1422 |pmid=21665743 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2002AmJB...89.1422C }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rodgers |first1=Vikki L. |last2=Wolfe |first2=Benjamin E. |last3=Werden |first3=Leland K. |last4=Finzi |first4=Adrien C. |date=September 2008 |title=The invasive species ''Alliaria petiolata'' (garlic mustard) increases soil nutrient availability in northern hardwood-conifer forests |journal=Oecologia |volume=157 |issue=3 |pages=459–471 |bibcode=2008Oecol.157..459R |doi=10.1007/s00442-008-1089-8 |pmid=18612654 |s2cid=13475605}}</ref>

The plant is classified as an [[invasive species]] in North America. Since being brought to the United States by settlers, it has [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] and expanded its range to include most of the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast]] and [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]], as well as south-eastern Canada.<ref>{{cite web |author=USDA NRCS National Plant Data Team |title=Alliaria petiolata (M. Bieb.) Cavara & Grande |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=ALPE4 |access-date=13 May 2022 |website=USDA Plants Database |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture}}</ref> It is one of the few invasive herbaceous species able to dominate the [[understory]] of North American forests and has thus reduced the [[biodiversity]] of many areas.<ref name="Garlic Mustard" />

Of the many natural enemies it has in its native range, several have been tested for use as [[Biological pest control|biological control agents]]. Five weevil species from the genus ''[[Ceutorhynchus]]'' and one [[flea beetle]] were selected as candidates for preliminary testing in the 1990s. Since that time, those studying the candidates have narrowed the list to two or three weevils. Despite the demonstrated effectiveness of ''C. scrobicollis'' and ''C. constrictus'' in field testing, the importation and release of biological control agents such as those has been repeatedly blocked by the USDA's TAG (Technical Advisory Group). In particular, ''C. scrobicollis'', which is [[monophagous]] and has been specifically studied since 2002, continues to be blocked, despite researchers' many petitions for approval.<ref name="Landis">{{cite web |last=Landis |first=Doug |title=Management Options |url=http://www.ipm.msu.edu/invasive_species/garlic_mustard/management_options |access-date=10 September 2017 |website=Integrated Pest Management |publisher=Michigan State University}}</ref><ref name="Reardon 2017">{{cite web |last=Reardon |first=Richard |title=FHTET Biological Control Program – Sponsored Projects |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/foresthealth/technology/pdfs/bc_prog_update_10_16.pdf |access-date=10 September 2017 |website=FHTET Biological Control Program |publisher=USDA Forest Service}}</ref> It is currently estimated that adequate control of garlic mustard can be achieved by the introduction of just two weevils, with ''C. scrobicollis'' being the most important of the two.<ref name="lccmr.leg.mn">Becker, R., 2017. Implementing Biological Control of Garlic Mustard – Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund 2017 RFP. http://www.lccmr.leg.mn/proposals/2017/original/107-d.pdf</ref> None of the roughly 76 species that control this plant in its native range has been approved for introduction as of 2018 and federal agencies continue to use more traditional forms of control, such as chemical herbicides.<ref name="Thiele WOSU">{{cite news |last1=Thiele |first1=Rebecca |date=5 January 2018 |title=Invasive Garlic Mustard: Love It Or Leave It? |url=https://news.wosu.org/news/2018-01-05/invasive-garlic-mustard-love-it-or-leave-it |work=WOSU News}}</ref>

In North America, the plant offers very little wildlife benefits and is toxic to larvae of certain rarer butterfly species (e.g. ''[[Pieris oleracea]]'' and ''[[Pieris virginiensis]]'') that lay eggs on the plants, as it is related to native mustards but creates chemicals that they are not adapted to.<ref name="efotg.sc.egov.usda.gov">{{Cite web |title=Pest Management Invasive Plant Control – Garlic Mustard (''Alliara petiolata'') USDA NRCS Conservation Practice Job Sheet MN-797 |url=http://efotg.sc.egov.usda.gov/references/public/MN/GarlicMustardMN.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211162058/https://efotg.sc.egov.usda.gov/references/public/mn/garlicmustardmn.pdf |archive-date=11 February 2017 |access-date=27 May 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Davis |first1=Samantha |title=Evaluating Threats to the Rare Butterfly, ''Pieris Virginiensis'' |date=1 January 2015 |url=https://corescholar.libraries.wright.edu/etd_all/1433/}}</ref> They have also been known to inhibit growth of [[Ectomycorrhiza|ectomycorrhizal fungi]]. These fungi play many different roles in a forest ecosystem however inhibition by ''Alliaria petiolata,'' may impact tree seedlings in a given environment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wolfe |first1=Benjamin E. |last2=Rodgers |first2=Vikki L. |last3=Stinson |first3=Kristina A. |last4=Pringle |first4=Anne |date=2008-06-10 |title=The invasive plant ''Alliaria petiolata'' (garlic mustard) inhibits ectomycorrhizal fungi in its introduced range |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=96 |issue=4 |pages=777–783 |bibcode=2008JEcol..96..777W |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2008.01389.x |issn=0022-0477}}</ref> Though this plant does have antimicrobial properties, it has an overall weak effect on bacterial communities found in soil, which only occurs under temporally specific conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burke |first1=David J. |last2=Chan |first2=Charlotte R. |date=January 2010 |title=Effects of the invasive plant garlic mustard (''Alliaria petiolata'') on bacterial communities in a northern hardwood forest soil |journal=Canadian Journal of Microbiology |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=81–86 |doi=10.1139/w09-100 |issn=0008-4166 |pmid=20130698}}</ref>  

Native species, including two stem-mining weevils, a stem-mining fly, a leaf-mining fly, a scale insect, two fungi, and aphids (taxonomic identification for all species is pending) were found attacking garlic mustard in North America. However, their attacks were of little consequence to plant performance or reproduction of garlic mustard.<ref name="Garlic Mustard" />

== Toxicity ==
Young first-year garlic mustard plants contain up to 100'' ''ppm [[cyanide]], a level which is toxic to many vertebrates.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cipollini |first1=Don |last2=Gruner |first2=Bill |date=19 December 2006 |title=Cyanide in the Chemical Arsenal of Garlic Mustard, Alliaria petiolata |journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=85–94 |bibcode=2006JCEco..33...85C |doi=10.1007/s10886-006-9205-x |pmid=17146719 |s2cid=34736542}}</ref> Once the plant is chopped up, the cyanide gas is eliminated.<ref>{{cite web |last=Main |first=Douglas |date=April 26, 2021 |title=Invasive garlic mustard hurts native species—but its harmful powers wane over time |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/garlic-mustard-toxic-invader-power-waning-edible-cyanide |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426215048/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/article/garlic-mustard-toxic-invader-power-waning-edible-cyanide |archive-date=26 April 2021 |access-date=May 2, 2022 |publisher=[[National Geographic]] |quote=...the cyanide is easily sidestepped by chopping up the plant, which releases most of the gas in a few minutes.}}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==
Garlic mustard is one of the oldest spices used in Europe. [[Phytolith]]s in pottery of the [[Ertebølle culture|Ertebølle]] and [[Funnelbeaker culture|Funnelneck-Beaker culture]] in north-eastern Germany and Denmark, dating to 4100–3750 [[BCE]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Saul |first1=Hayley |last2=Madella |first2=Marco |last3=Fischer |first3=Anders |last4=Glykou |first4=Aikaterini |last5=Hartz |first5=Sönke |last6=Craig |first6=Oliver E. |title=Phytoliths in Pottery Reveal the Use of Spice in European Prehistoric Cuisine |journal=PLOS ONE |date=21 August 2013 |volume=8 |issue=8 |article-number=e70583 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0070583 |pmid=23990910 |pmc=3749173 |bibcode=2013PLoSO...870583S |doi-access=free }}</ref> indicate its use in that era.

In 17th-century Britain, it was recommended as a flavouring for salt fish. It can also be made into a sauce for eating with roast lamb or salad.<ref name="Reader 2001">''[[Reader's Digest]] Nature Lover's Library, Field Guide to the Wildflowers of Britain'', Editor Michael W. Davison, Art Editor Neal V. Martin, The Reader's Digest Association Limited, 11 Westferry Circus, [[Canary Wharf]], London E144HE, Reprint 2001, {{ISBN|0 276 42506 5}}{{page needed|date=August 2021}}</ref> Early European settlers brought the herb to the [[New World]] to use as a garlic-type flavouring. Its traditional medicinal purposes include use as a [[diuretic]].<ref name="S&S" /> The herb was also planted as a form of erosion control.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kleinstein |first1=Debby |title=Introduced Species Summary Project Garlic Mustard (''Alliaria petiolata'') |url=http://www.columbia.edu/itc/cerc/danoff-burg/invasion_bio/inv_spp_summ/Alliaria_petiolata.html |access-date=19 May 2015}}</ref>

Today, the chopped leaves are used for flavouring in salads and sauces such as pesto, and sometimes the flowers and fruit are included as well. The leaves, best when young, taste of both garlic and mustard. The seeds are sometimes used in France to season food.<ref name="S&S">{{cite book |title=Simon & Schuster's Guide to Herbs and Spices |editor=Stanley Schuler |isbn=0-671-73489-X |author=Gualtiero Simonetti |year=1990 |publisher=Simon & Schuster, Inc |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/simonschustersgu0000simo }}</ref> Garlic mustard was once used medicinally<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ibiblio.org/pfaf/cgi-bin/arr_html?Alliaria+petiolata|url-status=unfit|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070814225031/http://www.ibiblio.org/pfaf/cgi-bin/arr_html?Alliaria+petiolata|archive-date=14 August 2007|work=Plants for a Future: Database Search|title=Alliaria petiolata}}</ref> as a disinfectant, and was sometimes used to treat wounds.<ref name="S&S" />
